title: Draft Counterclaim Against Plaintiff for Breach of Joint Development Agreement

blind.coverage:
I read all 73 criteria and the instructions. I read all 8 supplied documents in full: the complaint, JDA, MNDA, strategy memo, the Bellingham-DeLuca emails, the Ayers report, the Langford report, and the portal logs (every sheet). I also read the judge prompt, which asks for a literal pass/fail on each criterion, and the solver system prompt.

Things I noticed but did not flag:
- The memo gets the email authors wrong ("Marcus Bellingham (VP of Engineering)" and "Julia DeLuca (Director of Product Strategy)"). The emails show Craig Bellingham, Program Manager, and Martin DeLuca, CEO. The rubric uses the correct names from the emails, so this is a trap the rubric handles properly.
- The Langford and Ayers reports give different titles for the patent. No criterion tests the title.
- The patent claims the same features that the trade secret claim relies on (14 layers, 45 μm pitch, radial via pattern). No criterion forces that error.
- The same Rule 9(b) points are tested twice (C-041/069, C-042/071, C-043/070). That double-weights them but is not a defect.

Authorities: I read Express One v. Steinbeck on CourtListener. I read one passage of Trinseo v. Harper (5th Cir. 2026) and one of Title Source v. HouseCanary. I did not read Brand Services, Embarcadero, or Lifesize themselves. I did not check against primary text: the post-2021 scope of § 38.001, the Fifth Circuit's rules on enforcing jury waivers, the Texas rule that litigation fees are not recoverable as damages, or Texas's net-profits rule.

findings.title: Mandatory conversion count: Texas does not recognize conversion of intangible design files, and TUTSA likely preempts it
findings.explanation: C-049 fails any counterclaim that leaves out conversion. Texas does not recognize conversion of intangible property unless the right is merged into a document (Express One). Here Vasquez downloaded copies with her own portal credentials, and Vantage never lost possession of its files. Conversion based on trade-secret information is also routinely held preempted by TUTSA § 134A.007. The strategy memo recommends breach of the JDA, the DTSA, breach of the MNDA, fraudulent inducement, and alternative unjust enrichment. It never mentions conversion, and it warns that TUTSA may displace common-law claims resting on the same facts. So a careful drafter who drops conversion as not cognizable and preempted fails the all-pass metric. The case for requiring it: C-050 contemplates conversion pleaded 'to the extent not preempted', Rule 13(a) waiver pressure favors including more claims, and a few courts have entertained conversion of electronic data. That makes including it defensible, but making it mandatory is not.

evidence.quote: FAIL if no conversion claim is asserted.
If we include common-law claims grounded in the same conduct, we should plead them in the alternative or ensure they rest on independent factual grounds.
Authorized Lumenara Users' | B13='Elena Vasquez (LUMN-EVASQUEZ), Craig Bellingham (LUMN-CBELLING), Dr. Kevin Zhao (LUMN-KZHAO)

authorities.citation: Express One Int'l, Inc. v. Steinbeck, 53 S.W.3d 895, 901 (Tex. App.—Dallas 2001)
authorities.proposition: Texas law has never recognized conversion of intangible property except where an intangible right has been merged into a document and that document has been converted.

authorities.citation: Trinseo v. Harper, No. 24-20460 (5th Cir. Jan. 21, 2026)
authorities.proposition: Describes the Louisiana trade secrets act's preemption provision as substantively identical to TUTSA § 134A.007, and discusses preemption of conversion claims for confidential information that qualifies as a trade secret.

authorities.citation: Brand Servs., L.L.C. v. Irex Corp., 909 F.3d 151, 158–59 (5th Cir. 2018)
authorities.proposition: The Louisiana act (analogous to TUTSA) preempts conversion claims involving information that qualifies as a trade secret.

findings.suggested_fix: Make conversion optional. For example: PASS if conversion is either omitted, or pleaded in the alternative with acknowledgment of intangible-property and preemption limits. Or delete C-049.

findings.title: Requires $18,087,500 in 'compensatory damages', which counts litigation expert fees and a Northfield loss the JDA's damages exclusion bars for milestone breaches
findings.explanation:
C-054 requires total compensatory damages of about $18,087,500. That total includes $287,500 in Ridgeline and Hawksmere fees, and Hawksmere's share is for damages modeling for this lawsuit. Under Texas's American rule, litigation expert fees are not compensatory damages. They are recoverable as fees and costs under JDA § 13.5. A drafter who pleads $17.8M in damages and seeks the expert fees under § 13.5 could fail C-054, and fails C-065 if the $287,500 is not stated as a number.

The $8.7M Northfield figure is also a problem. It is gross contract value, not net profit. It comes from the § 6 milestone breaches, and JDA § 11.1 excludes 'LOSS OF BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES' except for § 7/§ 8 breaches or fraud or willful misconduct. It is also stacked on $3.4M of reliance (wasted-cost) damages on top of expectation damages.

At the pleading stage, adopting the expert's figures is tolerable, which is why this is arguable. But the rubric rewards adopting them without scrutiny and could fail a drafter who scrutinizes them.

evidence.quote: FAIL if the total compensatory damages figure is materially different from $18,087,500 or if the prayer does not quantify compensatory damages at all.
Vantage retained my firm to analyze and quantify the economic damages resulting from Lumenara's conduct.
LOSS OF REVENUE, LOSS OF BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES, LOSS OF DATA
the prevailing Party shall be entitled to recover from the non-prevailing Party its reasonable attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, consulting fees

authorities.citation: Tony Gullo Motors I, L.P. v. Chapa, 212 S.W.3d 299 (Tex. 2006)
authorities.proposition: Texas follows the American rule: attorney's fees are not recoverable unless a statute or contract provides for them.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept a compensatory total of about $17.8M when the $287,500 is sought as fees or costs, or accept an itemized request for either amount. Allow 'in an amount to be proven at trial' when the components are quantified elsewhere in the pleading.

findings.title: Jury demand is mandatory even though JDA § 13.3 waives jury trial for any counterclaim relating to the agreement
findings.explanation: JDA § 13.3 is a conspicuous, mutual, certified waiver of jury trial in any 'COUNTERCLAIM ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT'. Every one of Vantage's counterclaims relates to the JDA. Lumenara's own complaint (¶ 66) rests its claims on JDA § 7.3, so the waiver arguably reaches Lumenara's jury demand too. A strategically careful drafter might leave out a jury demand and instead preserve the right to enforce § 13.3, or might demand a jury only on claims outside the JDA. C-073 fails that choice. A demand 'on all issues so triable' is cheap and common, so this is arguable rather than problematic. The rubric never considers the waiver.

evidence.quote: ANY AND ALL RIGHTS IT MAY HAVE TO A TRIAL BY JURY IN ANY LEGAL PROCEEDING, ACTION, SUIT, OR COUNTERCLAIM ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT
unauthorized use of Lumenara's Background IP in violation of JDA Section 7.3
FAIL if no jury trial demand is included.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the pleading includes a jury demand, or explains the omission by addressing the JDA § 13.3 waiver.

findings.title: Texas fee criterion does not credit the JDA § 13.5 prevailing-party fee clause, which is the stronger basis
findings.explanation: C-060 fails a prayer that requests only DTSA fees 'with no reference to Texas law fee recovery.' A drafter who requests fees under JDA § 13.5 (prevailing-party fees, including expert and consulting fees) and under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D) has a stronger contract-fee basis than § 38.001. Section 13.5 is governed by Texas law (§ 13.1). A judge applying the criterion literally may still fail that prayer because it neither cites § 38.001 nor says 'as permitted by law.'

evidence.quote: FAIL if attorney's fees are not requested at all or if only DTSA fees are requested with no reference to Texas law fee recovery.
In any action, proceeding, or counterclaim brought to enforce any provision of this Agreement ... the prevailing Party shall be entitled to recover

findings.suggested_fix: Also accept a fee request based on JDA § 13.5, or on any contractual or Texas-law basis for the contract claims.

findings.title: Langford partly blames the February 2024 Northfield loss on M4, which was not due until March 31, 2024
findings.explanation: Langford says Vantage lost Northfield in February 2024 partly because it could not show manufacturing readiness, since Lumenara never delivered M4. But M4 was not due until March 31, 2024, after the contract was awarded. The memo repeats the idea that the loss followed from the project's failure. A correct counterclaim should tie Northfield to the M2 and M3 failures only. C-030 and C-052 are worded generally enough that they do not misgrade either way. But the record steers solvers toward a causal chain that cannot be true, and the rubric does not catch a drafter who copies it.

evidence.quote: because Lumenara never delivered Milestone 4 --- the production-ready coating process documentation, due March 31, 2024 --- Vantage was unable to demonstrate manufacturing readiness
In February 2024, Northfield Aerospace Solutions notified Vantage that the contract had been awarded to a competing bidder.

findings.suggested_fix: Fix the Langford report so the Northfield loss rests on M2 and M3 only, or move the M4 deadline before the award date.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound, and its facts match the primary documents. Dates, milestone figures, and the damages components all line up. It also correctly follows the emails, not the memo, on who wrote them and what their titles were. The one problematic criterion is C-049. It requires a conversion count that Texas does not recognize for intangible design files, and TUTSA would likely preempt it. The memo never recommends conversion, so a careful drafter who leaves it out fails the all-pass metric. Four more issues are arguable. C-054 and C-065 treat litigation expert fees as compensatory damages and adopt the Langford total without regard to the JDA's exclusion of lost business opportunities. C-073 requires a jury demand without considering the JDA's mutual jury waiver. C-060 does not credit the JDA's own fee clause. And the Langford report contains an impossible causal link for the Northfield loss. The remaining criteria are standard parts of a counterclaim or follow directly from the record and the memo.

sol_verdicts.sol_locator: Confirmed defects / forced questionable advocacy: item 1
sol_verdicts.reason: C-049 fails any pleading that leaves out conversion. Texas limits conversion of intangibles to rights merged into a document (Express One), TUTSA § 134A.007 displaces misappropriation-based torts, and the memo never recommends conversion. C-050 is different: it accepts many forms of handling preemption, including independent factual framing. It only fails common-law claims pleaded with no qualification. On its own it is sound, though it should be conformed if C-049 becomes optional.

sol_verdicts.sol_locator: Confirmed defects / forced questionable advocacy: item 2
sol_verdicts.reason: Langford ¶ 117 uses the full $8.7M contract value rather than net profit. Langford ¶ 111 blames the February 2024 award on M4, which was not due until March 31, 2024. So the source figures are flawed. But pleading a retained expert's quantified figure in a prayer is common, and it is not legally wrong at the pleading stage. JDA § 11.1 also exempts fraud and willful misconduct, which are pleaded here. The criteria reward the flawed total and could fail a drafter who pleads net damages, but they do not misgrade most competent drafts.

sol_verdicts.sol_locator: Confirmed defects / forced questionable advocacy: item 3
sol_verdicts.reason: The memo says unjust enrichment is 'worth considering' and that the team 'should consider adding' it (D.2). It flags TUTSA displacement right after (D.3). Texas generally bars unjust enrichment where a valid express contract covers the subject, and neither side disputes the JDA or MNDA. Alternative pleading is cheap and the memo leans toward it, so requiring it is defensible. But it is discretionary, and a reasoned omission should not zero the run.

Langford line 155 treats $287,500 in Ridgeline and Hawksmere fees as consequential damages. Hawksmere's share is litigation damages modeling. Under the American rule these are fees and costs, recoverable under JDA § 13.5, not compensatory damages. A drafter who seeks them under § 13.5 and pleads about $17.8M in compensatory damages risks failing C-054. C-065 only asks that the fees be quantified, so it is milder.

Langford line 139 states $5,680,000 and rounds it to $5.7M. The exact sum is $18,067,500, which differs from $18,087,500 by about 0.1%. C-053 and C-064 say 'approximately' and C-054 accepts 'minor rounding differences', so the rounding is not a defect. I list C-054 as arguable only on the separate damages-composition grounds in O2.

The record supports a promissory-fraud theory without inventing facts. DeLuca signed the JDA as CEO, which is the promise made with no intent to perform. Bellingham was the program manager and negotiator. DeLuca's May 16 email directs the team to 'demonstrate good faith' externally and to finalize signing on June 1. The memo expressly asks for this count, and C-041 allows 'and/or other Lumenara representatives.' These are standard Rule 9(b) elements.

The memo does not list a patent count. But it tells the team to 'independently evaluate whether other theories are available,' and the Ayers report (§ 8, Opinion 3) compares Claim 1 element by element and concludes the LumiSense 400 practices '287 at least the independent claims. JDA § 13.2 expressly contemplates patent infringement claims. A competent drafter would plead it. Sol's point that the patent was not independently verified is not a rubric defect.

findings.title: Mandatory conversion count: Texas does not recognize conversion of intangible design files, and TUTSA likely displaces it
findings.explanation: C-049 fails any counterclaim without a conversion count. Texas does not recognize conversion of intangible property unless the right is merged into a document (Express One). Vasquez downloaded copies with her own authorized credentials, and Vantage never lost possession of its files. Conversion resting on trade-secret misappropriation is also displaced by TUTSA § 134A.007. The memo recommends breach of the JDA, the DTSA, breach of the MNDA, fraudulent inducement, and alternative unjust enrichment. It never mentions conversion, and D.3 warns about displacement. A careful drafter who omits conversion fails the all-pass metric. Including it 'to the extent not preempted' is defensible, and C-050 contemplates that. Making it mandatory is not. C-050 itself is sound, but it should be conformed so that omitting both common-law claims passes.

evidence.quote: FAIL if no conversion claim is asserted.
may displace certain common-law claims based on the same conduct underlying a trade secret misappropriation claim
Authorized Lumenara Users' | B13='Elena Vasquez (LUMN-EVASQUEZ)

authorities.citation: Express One Int'l, Inc. v. Steinbeck, 53 S.W.3d 895, 901 (Tex. App.—Dallas 2001)

findings.suggested_fix: Make conversion optional. PASS if conversion is omitted, or if it is pleaded with acknowledgment of the intangible-property and preemption limits. Conform C-050 so that omitting both common-law claims passes.

findings.title: Damages criteria require Langford's $18,087,500 total, including gross Northfield revenue and litigation expert fees
findings.explanation: C-054 requires a total compensatory figure of about $18,087,500. C-052 requires about $8.7M for Northfield. Langford ¶ 117 applies the full contract value with no deduction of saved costs, but Texas lost profits are net profits. Langford also stacks $3.4M in reliance (wasted-cost) damages on top of this expectation measure. The total includes $287,500 in Ridgeline and Hawksmere fees, which Langford calls 'consequential damages.' Hawksmere's share is litigation damages modeling. Those fees are recoverable as fees and costs under JDA § 13.5, not as compensatory damages. A drafter who pleads net lost profits 'in an amount to be proven', or who moves the $287,500 into the § 13.5 fee request, risks failing C-054 and possibly C-052. C-065 only requires quantification, which is milder. This is arguable, not problematic: pleading a retained expert's figures in a prayer is common, and JDA § 11.1 exempts fraud and willful misconduct. The rounding difference ($5.68M vs $5.7M) is not a defect.

evidence.quote: I apply the full contract value of \$8.7 million rather than a discounted figure.
These costs are recoverable as consequential damages proximately caused by Lumenara's breaches
the prevailing Party shall be entitled to recover from the non-prevailing Party its reasonable attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, consulting fees

authorities.citation: Tony Gullo Motors I, L.P. v. Chapa, 212 S.W.3d 299 (Tex. 2006)
authorities.proposition: Texas follows the American rule: fees are not recoverable unless a statute or contract provides for them.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept a quantified compensatory total of about $17.8M when the $287,500 is sought as fees or costs under § 13.5. Accept Northfield pleaded as net lost profits on an $8.7M contract, in an amount to be proven.

findings.title: Unjust enrichment is mandatory though the memo only says to 'consider' it and flags displacement
findings.explanation: C-048 fails any counterclaim without an alternative unjust-enrichment count. The memo frames it as optional ('worth considering', 'should consider adding') and then flags TUTSA displacement for exactly this theory. Texas generally bars unjust enrichment where a valid express contract covers the subject. Here neither side disputes the JDA or the MNDA; Lumenara sues on the MNDA. A drafter who makes a reasoned decision to rely on the contract, DTSA, and fraud counts fails the all-pass metric. This is arguable rather than problematic because alternative pleading costs little, Rule 13(a) favors including more, and the memo leans toward including it.

evidence.quote: We should consider adding this as an alternative count in the counterclaim.
FAIL if unjust enrichment is not asserted at all

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if unjust enrichment is pleaded in the alternative, or omitted with the contract, DTSA, and fraud theories covering the same benefit.

findings.title: Jury demand is mandatory although JDA § 13.3 mutually waives jury trial for related counterclaims
findings.explanation: JDA § 13.3 is a conspicuous, mutual, certified waiver of jury trial for any 'COUNTERCLAIM ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT.' Every count here relates to the JDA. Lumenara demanded a jury anyway. A drafter who prefers to enforce § 13.3 and seek a bench trial, or who relies on Lumenara's Rule 38 demand, fails C-073. A protective demand 'on all issues so triable' is cheap and customary, so most competent drafts pass. That makes this arguable rather than problematic. The rubric never considers the waiver.

findings.title: Texas fee criterion may fail a fee request based on JDA § 13.5 rather than § 38.001
findings.explanation: C-060 fails a prayer that requests only DTSA fees 'with no reference to Texas law fee recovery.' A drafter who requests fees under JDA § 13.5 (the Texas-law-governed prevailing-party clause, which also covers expert and consulting fees) and under § 1836(b)(3)(D) has a strong contract basis. A literal judge may still fail it, because it neither cites § 38.001 nor uses a general 'as permitted by law' formula.

evidence.quote: FAIL if attorney's fees are not requested at all or if only DTSA fees are requested with no reference to Texas law fee recovery.
In any action, proceeding, or counterclaim brought to enforce any provision of this Agreement

findings.suggested_fix: Also accept a fee request based on JDA § 13.5 or any other contractual or Texas-law basis for the contract counts.

final.changes_from_blind: I adopted C-048 (unjust enrichment made mandatory) as arguable after reading Sol. The memo only says to 'consider' the count and flags displacement for it, which is the same discretionary-count problem as conversion, only weaker. I broadened blind O2 to state the gross-revenue versus net-profit problem in Northfield explicitly, citing Langford ¶ 117, and it now links to Sol's damages items. I kept it arguable rather than adopting Sol's 'confirmed', because pleading an expert's quantified figures is ordinary practice at the pleading stage and JDA § 11.1 exempts fraud. I rejected Sol's C-050 as a standalone defect, the rounding point (C-053/C-064), the fraud Rule 9(b) cluster (the record shows DeLuca signed the JDA and directed an external show of good faith), and the patent cluster (Ayers § 8 supplies a claim comparison). I kept all five blind findings, renumbered as O1, O2, O4, O5, O6.
final.overall: The rubric's facts are largely accurate. Dates, milestones, parties, and damages figures match the primary documents, and it correctly follows the emails, not the memo, on who wrote them and their titles. The one problematic criterion is C-049. It makes conversion mandatory, but Texas does not recognize conversion of intangible design files copied through authorized access, TUTSA likely displaces it, and the memo never recommends it. Five issues are arguable. C-052, C-054, and C-065 adopt Langford's gross-revenue Northfield figure and treat litigation expert fees as compensatory damages. C-048 makes a discretionary unjust-enrichment count mandatory. C-073 requires a jury demand despite the JDA's mutual waiver. C-060 does not credit the JDA § 13.5 fee clause. And the Langford report contains an impossible M4 causal link for the Northfield loss. Sol's fraud and patent concerns do not hold up against the record.
final.coverage: I reviewed all 73 criteria and the instructions. In this pass I re-read the key parts of the documents: the strategy memo sections III to V, both emails in full, the JDA's §§ 5, 6, 11, and 13 and its signature blocks, Langford ¶¶ 107–157 and the summary, Ayers § 8, and the complaint's counts and jury demand. The blind pass covered all 8 documents in full. I read Sol's audit and index, and I gave a verdict on each of Sol's 7 items against the record. For authorities, I read Express One on CourtListener in the blind pass. I did not read the primary text of TUTSA § 134A.007 or Tony Gullo in this session.
